title: Identify and interpret related legislation and its impact on the team, department or division and ensure compliance

lessons.title: Identifying legislation that applies to your team
lessons.html:
Why managers must know the law

Every agricultural team, whether a farm production unit, a packhouse, an extension office or a co-operative, operates within a framework of legislation. As a team leader or manager you are responsible for knowing which laws apply, what they require, and making sure your team complies. Ignorance of the law is not a defence, and non-compliance can lead to injuries, fines, prosecution, lost market access and damage to reputation.

Common legislation in South African agriculture

AreaLegislation
Health and safetyOccupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993
Employment conditionsBasic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and the sectoral determination for farm workers
Labour relationsLabour Relations Act 66 of 1995
EquityEmployment Equity Act 55 of 1998
Personal informationProtection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013
Agricultural chemicalsFertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947
Natural resourcesConservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983; National Water Act 36 of 1998
Animal health and welfareAnimal Diseases Act 35 of 1984; Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962
Meat safetyMeat Safety Act 40 of 2000

Not every law applies to every team. A packhouse team is affected by food safety and OHS requirements; a livestock team by animal health and welfare laws; an extension office by POPIA when it stores farmer records.

How to identify relevant legislation

  1. List your team's activities, inputs, outputs and risks.
  2. For each, ask which laws, regulations, municipal by-laws and industry standards apply.
  3. Consult reliable sources: the Government Gazette, department websites, your organisation's legal or HR department, industry bodies and labour inspectors.
  4. Include regulations made under each Act and any sectoral determinations, as these often contain the detailed requirements.
  5. Record the results in a legal register with the law, its relevance, the responsible person and the date last reviewed.

lessons.title: Interpreting legislation and its impact
lessons.html:
From legal text to practical meaning

Legislation is written in formal language. Your task is to interpret what it means for your team's daily work. This does not mean giving legal opinions; it means understanding obligations well enough to act on them and knowing when to ask a legal expert.

Reading legislation effectively

  • Start with the purpose and definitions sections. Definitions often decide whether the law applies to you, for example who counts as an employer or employee.
  • Identify duties: what must be done, by whom, and by when.
  • Identify prohibitions: what must never be done.
  • Note required records, registrations, permits and reports.
  • Note the consequences of non-compliance.
  • Look for regulations and codes of practice that give detail.

Where meaning is unclear, consult your HR, legal or compliance function, or an inspector. Use official summaries and guides from government departments, but check that they are current.

Assessing impact on the team

For each relevant law, analyse how it affects the team in these areas:

AreaExample of impact
Work proceduresOHS requirements mean spraying may only be done by trained workers with the correct PPE, following the product label
People and rolesHealth and safety representatives must be designated where the law requires them
TrainingWorkers need training on hazards, chemicals and machinery
RecordsAttendance, working hours, leave, chemical application and incident records must be kept
CostsPPE, training, minimum wage increases and permit fees affect the budget
Information handlingPOPIA requires farmer and worker personal information to be collected for a clear purpose and kept secure

Legislation changes. Minimum wages are adjusted, regulations are amended and new laws are passed. Assign someone to monitor changes and review the legal register at least once a year.

Communicate impacts to the team in plain language. Explain not only what the rule is but why it exists, for example to protect workers' health or the farm's export market.

lessons.title: Ensuring and monitoring compliance
lessons.html:
Building compliance into daily work

Compliance is not a once-off exercise before an audit. It must be part of how the team works every day. As a manager you translate legal requirements into procedures, responsibilities and checks.

Steps to ensure compliance

  1. Develop or update procedures: write standard operating procedures that include legal requirements, such as safe chemical storage, working hours scheduling or handling of farmer data.
  2. Assign responsibility: each requirement in the legal register must have a named owner.
  3. Train the team: explain the requirements and procedures, and keep training records.
  4. Provide resources: PPE, safe storage, first aid kits, secure filing and time for training.
  5. Keep records: records are your evidence of compliance during inspections and audits.

Monitoring

Use checklists, regular inspections and internal audits. Walk through the workplace and observe whether procedures are followed. Check records for completeness. Encourage workers to report hazards and concerns without fear of victimisation. Track incidents and near-misses and investigate their causes.

Dealing with non-compliance

When you find non-compliance, act promptly:

  • Stop any activity that poses immediate danger to people, animals or the environment.
  • Find the root cause: lack of knowledge, missing resources, unclear procedures or deliberate disregard.
  • Take corrective action and set a deadline.
  • Apply your organisation's disciplinary procedures fairly where rules were knowingly broken, following the Labour Relations Act and your code of conduct.
  • Report to senior management as required, and to authorities where the law requires reporting, for example certain incidents or notifiable animal diseases.

Cooperate openly with inspectors. Prepare records in advance and accompany inspectors during visits.

Key points

  • Identify all legislation relevant to your team's activities and record it in a legal register.
  • Read definitions, duties, prohibitions and record requirements; ask experts when unclear.
  • Assess impact on procedures, people, training, records, costs and information handling.
  • Turn requirements into procedures with named owners, training and records.
  • Monitor regularly and correct non-compliance promptly, stopping any dangerous activity.

quiz.question: Which Act deals with occupational health and safety in South Africa?

options.text: Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993

quiz.question: An extension office stores farmers' personal contact details. Which Act is most directly relevant?

options.text: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013
Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983
A list of lawyers the company uses
A record of relevant laws, their relevance, responsible persons and review dates

Ignore it if the job is nearly done
